events.name: Arthur Donaldson's School for People of Colour: scholars, 1809-1813
events.description: Arthur Donaldson opened his school for children of colour on May 1, 1809, in Front Street between Arch and Race, with four scholars, 'convinced that I could not be employed in any way more useful, than instructing the descendants of Africa in plain learning, (as I observed a great want of Schools for them).' An accidental fire on October 23, 1811 burned his schoolroom with all its desks, benches and books (a loss he put at $300) and his list of scholars, so the earliest lists were written 'as near as can be recollected.' He reopened five days later at the corner of Wood and Crown streets, moved on January 1, 1812 to Fifth above Race, and in September 1812 (the magazine's erratum corrects '7th mo.' to '9th mo.') to Nicholson's Court, or Malt Alley, back of No. 107 Cherry Alley, behind the Plaster of Paris Mill on Race above Sixth. By then 93 were on the list (50 boys, 43 girls), about 60 attending. On May 12, 1813 he counted 107 (55 boys, 52 girls). He had three assistants: boys learned from the alphabet through the spelling book downstairs, then reading, writing and cyphering; girls also learned needlework under 'a well qualified Mistress.' Books: Comly's Spelling Book and its Sequel, the Introduction to the English Reader and Sequel, and Bennet's and Kimber's arithmetics. A night school ran alongside the day school. He printed the rolls so his pupils could learn to spell their own and one another's names and, 'when you come to be men and women, ... see how your fellow scholars have turned out.' The rolls: boys and girls from the opening to the fire; boys and girls who entered from October 28, 1811 to May 1, 1813; men and women of the night school; and the roll 'as they now stand, 5th Month 1st, 1813,' with those entering to July 1, ranked by class (arithmetic, writing, or not yet writing). Night scholars were probably adults. Each scholar's lists are given in their role. Where Julie Winch made a record for a scholar ('Attended Donaldson's school, 1809-13'; her notes run through surnames A-G) the scholar is linked to it; other scholars have their own records and are not linked to later adults of the same name. Donations: $31.50 in books and cash, and $97.67 subscribed after the fire (including $77.67 'collected by D. and J.'). Donaldson also asked why the Pennsylvania act of April 4, 1809 for educating poor children gratis was not applied to coloured children, and offered room for 200 to 300 scholars. Source: The Juvenile Magazine, No. 3 (Philadelphia: Arthur Donaldson, Seventh Month [July] 1st, 1813), from the Boston Public Library copy, courtesy the Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/sim_juvenile-magazine_1813_1-4_3). Michiko Quinones found this source through the Bernice Dutrieuille Shelton papers at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (https://discover.hsp.org/Record/ead-MSS131/Details). events.name: Schools for people of colour in Philadelphia, 1811 and 1813 (Arthur Donaldson's survey)
events.description: Arthur Donaldson visited every school for people of colour in Philadelphia twice and printed the counts. OCTOBER 26, 1811 (during the three days his school was closed by the fire): Willing's Alley school, free, under the monthly meetings of Friends, 50 boys and 54 girls, plus a free night school supported by an association of young men, about 60 in winter; one in Green's Court above Pine, boys and girls, about 50, and a night school of about 30; one in Sixth above South, 20; one in Lombard above Seventh, about 30; one in Seventh near Shippen, about 30; one in Sixth near South, about 20; one in Race below Fifth, about 20; his own, about 50, and a night school of 12. Total taught: 426. MAY 12, 1813, 'having visited them myself this day': 1. Willing's Alley, boys taught by Zebulon Holmes and girls by Mary Walton, under the care of the Monthly Meetings of Philadelphia, free, established 1771: 48 boys, 48 girls. 2. Quomony Clarkson, in Green's Court between Spruce and Pine, established 1804: 31 boys, 19 girls. 3. One in Sixth Street taught by Jane Hut, established 1803: 9 boys, 13 girls. 4. In Seventh below Shippen, John Gloster's [John Gloucester], established 1810: 16 boys, 11 girls. 5. In Lombard Street, established by Solomon Clarkson, October 27, 1812: 19 boys, 5 girls. 6. In Race Street, reading and sewing taught by Ruth Hand, supported by a fund belonging to the Episcopal Church under three trustees, established about 1786: 7 boys, 29 girls. 7. In Cherry Alley, taught by James Kelly, established by the Abolition Society March 1, 1813, free: 52 boys. 8. His own, established May 1, 1809: 55 boys, 52 girls. Total: eight schools, 237 males and 177 females, 414 in all. Zebulon Holmes, Mary Walton, Jane Hut and James Kelly are named here as text only. Source: The Juvenile Magazine, No. 3 (Philadelphia: Arthur Donaldson, Seventh Month [July] 1st, 1813), from the Boston Public Library copy, courtesy the Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/sim_juvenile-magazine_1813_1-4_3). Michiko Quinones found this source through the Bernice Dutrieuille Shelton papers at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (https://discover.hsp.org/Record/ead-MSS131/Details). events.name: Churches of the people of colour in Philadelphia, May 1813 (Juvenile Magazine)
events.description: 'An account of the religious denominations of coloured people in the City of Philadelphia, at this time': 1. Episcopal Church of St. Thomas: 180 members at its beginning, July 17, 1794; 560 on May 14, 1813. Absalom Jones, Rector. 2. Bethel Church, established July 28, 1784 [as printed]; 1,272 members on May 17, 1813; in South Sixth between Lombard and Pine. 3. Zoar Meeting, in Brown Street, Northern Liberties, established December 20, 1804, under the care of St. George's; 80 members. 4. Presbyterian Church, incorporated 1809; 300 members; the church built in 1810 in Seventh Street below Shippen. 5. First Baptist, established April 23, 1809, between Race and Vine and Ninth and Tenth streets, in Spring Garden; 80 members. 6. Union Methodist Meeting, under the charge of Bethel, established 1813; 74 members; in Coats' Street between old and new Fourth Street. 7. Mount Sion, under the care of the Episcopal Church, in St. John's Street near Peg's Run. 8. Frankford, under the charge of Bethel, established 1813; 36 members. Aggregate 2,366. PASTORS OF EACH DENOMINATION, PLACES OF ABODE (p. 72): Absalom Jones (Episcopal Church), Powel St. No. 32; Richard Allen (Bethel), Spruce Street No. 150; John Gloster [Gloucester] (Presbyterian), S. Seventh St., 5th door from Shippen Street; John King (1st Baptist), in 10th St. between Race and Vine. Source: The Juvenile Magazine, No. 3 (Philadelphia: Arthur Donaldson, Seventh Month [July] 1st, 1813), from the Boston Public Library copy, courtesy the Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/sim_juvenile-magazine_1813_1-4_3). events.name: Benevolent societies of the people of colour, 1813 (Juvenile Magazine)
events.description: 'An account of the Benevolent Societies established among the coloured people': 1. The Friendly Society, established 1796, 85 members. 2. Female Society, the Daughters of Ethiopia, established January 8, 1811, 30 members. 3. Female Society, the Daughters of Samaria, established June 10, 1812, 24 members. 4. The Benezette Philanthropic Society, established June 18, 1812, 52 members. 5. Farmers and Mechanics, established January 18, 1812, about 36 members. 6. The Female Benevolent Society, established November 3, 1803, 95 members. 7. The Angola Society, established November 1808, 26 members. 8. The Sons of St. Thomas, established February 15, 1812, 28 members. 9. St. James's Society, established February 14, 1812, 11 members. 10. The Sons of Africa, established March 6, 1810, 49 members. 11. African Lodge, No. 459, established June 24, 1809, 514 members [as printed; the stated aggregate of 590 works only if the lodge had 154]. Aggregate 590 members. 'The above societies meet and pay monthly subscriptions, for the purpose of assisting one another in case of sickness, as well as the widows and orphan children of members.' Also: the Union Society, for the support of schools and domestic manufactures, for the benefit of the African race and people of colour, established 1810. Source: The Juvenile Magazine, No. 3 (Philadelphia: Arthur Donaldson, Seventh Month [July] 1st, 1813), from the Boston Public Library copy, courtesy the Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/sim_juvenile-magazine_1813_1-4_3).
